precepts.text: At the end of every seven years, in the year of release, read the law at the feast of tabernacles.
precepts.point: A Hebrew servant goes free in the seventh year and is furnished liberally from the flock, the floor and the winepress.

note.label: Jubilee: The Year To Be Set Free

precepts.why:
“At the end of every seven years, in the solemnity of the year of release, in the feast of tabernacles”. Moses ties the year of release to a set time: every seventh year, in the feast of tabernacles. In that solemnity the land was released, the servants were released, and the debt was released.

It comes right after the Sabbath of the land in Leviticus 25. When the people ask, “What shall we eat the seventh year? behold, we shall not sow, nor gather in our increase”, God answers, “Then I will command my blessing upon you in the sixth year, and it shall bring forth fruit for three years.” Think about that with the seventh day Sabbath. Brothers and sisters say, I have to work on the Sabbath because that is my money day; that is the same question as verse 20, and it shows you do not believe what was read. Work six days and rest on the Sabbath, and the Most High will provide.

Deuteronomy 15:1 then goes into more detail on what that year of release in Deuteronomy 31:10 is: “At the end of every seven years thou shalt make a release”, and every creditor that lends to his neighbour, his brother, shall release it, “because it is called the Lord’s release.” Lend something, and at the end of seven years that debt is taken care of.

precepts.text: Ye have the poor always with you.
precepts.point: A Hebrew servant goes free in the seventh year and is furnished liberally from the flock, the floor and the winepress.

note.label: Jubilee: The Year To Be Set Free

precepts.why:
Deuteronomy 15:11 says, “For the poor shall never cease out of the land”, and Christ said the same: “For ye have the poor always with you; but me ye have not always.”

Notice what that tells us. In verses 5 and 6 the Lord promised that if we carefully hearken to observe all the commandments, “thou shalt lend unto many nations, but thou shalt not borrow; and thou shalt reign over many nations, but they shall not reign over thee.” That happened in the time of David and Solomon. There would even be no poor among us. But in verse 11 he says the poor shall never cease out of the land. The Lord was letting us know we were not going to be keeping those commandments too long.

So the command stands: “Thou shalt open thine hand wide unto thy brother, to thy poor, and to thy needy, in thy land.” If there be a poor man of one of thy brethren, “thou shalt not harden thine heart, nor shut thine hand from thy poor brother”, but lend him sufficient for his need. And beware of the wicked thought, “The seventh year, the year of release, is at hand”: imagine it is the sixth year, and you refuse your brother because in twelve months you will not get it back. If he cries unto the Lord against thee, “it be sin unto thee.” Give, and do not be grieved, and the Lord will bless you in all your works.

This is also why the Hebrew servant sold to you, a brother who was poor and lacked food, water and shelter, served only six years and was not sent away empty, but furnished liberally out of the flock, the floor and the winepress, so he or she could have a fresh start and be self-sufficient. It is because we were bondmen in Egypt and the Lord redeemed us. All the laws intertwine with love thy neighbour as thyself.

precepts.text: An Hebrew man or an Hebrew woman sold unto thee serves six years, and in the seventh year thou shalt let him go free.
precepts.point: Zedekiah's covenant in Jeremiah confirms the law in the prophets: every man was to let his Hebrew manservant and maidservant go free at the appointed release.

note.label: Exodus 21: The Judgments Set Before Israel

precepts.why:
Deuteronomy repeats the same judgment: “And if thy brother, an Hebrew man, or an Hebrew woman, be sold unto thee, and serve thee six years; then in the seventh year thou shalt let him go free from thee.” Six years he serves, and in the seventh he goes out free for nothing, and it is written for the Hebrew woman as well as the man.

If he came in by himself he goes out by himself; if he were married when he came in, his wife goes out with him. But if the master gave him a wife and she bare him sons or daughters, the wife and her children are the master’s and he goes out by himself, for he did not bring them in. Then he has two choices: go out alone, or plainly say, “I love my master, my wife, and my children; I will not go out free”, have his ear bored through with an aul at the door post, and serve his master for ever.

precepts.text: The unclean and the clean person shall eat it alike, as the roebuck and as the hart; the unclean and clean here are persons.
precepts.point: The unclean and the clean that may eat thereof are unclean and clean persons, not unclean meats; Israel had servants then and will have servants again.

note.label: Deuteronomy 12: The Place Where the Lord Puts His Name

precepts.why:
“Thou shalt eat it within thy gates: the unclean and the clean person shall eat it alike, as the roebuck, and as the hart.” Here the same words are spelled out: the unclean and the clean are persons. So when Deuteronomy 12:15 says “the unclean and the clean may eat thereof, as of the roebuck, and as of the hart”, the unclean and the clean that may eat are unclean and clean persons, not unclean meats.

Israel had servants then and will have servants again; clean and unclean persons alike could eat the flesh killed in the gates, as the roebuck and as the hart. The verse is not opening the door to unclean meat; it is saying who may eat.

precepts.text: The land keeps a sabbath unto the Lord: six years thou shalt sow thy field, but in the seventh year is a sabbath of rest unto the land.
precepts.point: Of a foreigner thou mayest exact it again, but that which is thine with thy brother thine hand shall release. The seven year release stands on the sabbath of the land already given in Leviticus 25.

note.label: Deuteronomy 15: The Year of Release and the Hebrew Servant

precepts.why:
The seven year release stands on the sabbath of the land already given in Leviticus 25. “When ye come into the land which I give you, then shall the land keep a sabbath unto the Lord. Six years thou shalt sow thy field, and six years thou shalt prune thy vineyard, and gather in the fruit thereof; But in the seventh year shall be a sabbath of rest unto the land, a sabbath for the Lord: thou shalt neither sow thy field, nor prune thy vineyard.”

Six years of sowing and a seventh of rest is the same count as “At the end of every seven years thou shalt make a release.” In the year the land rests, every creditor releases what he lent his neighbour, and “shall not exact it of his neighbour, or of his brother; because it is called the Lord’s release.”

Of a foreigner thou mayest exact it again, but that which is thine with thy brother thine hand shall release.

precepts.text: The Lord shall open unto thee his good treasure, and thou shalt lend unto many nations and shalt not borrow; the blessing Israel forfeited by breaking the commandments.
precepts.point: This is the blessing that was to come upon us. Since we broke the commandments of the Most High, the other nations lend to us and we borrow from them; we go to them for loans and everything else.

note.label: Deuteronomy 15: The Year of Release and the Hebrew Servant

precepts.why:
The promise of verse 6 stands among the blessings of chapter 28: “The Lord shall open unto thee his good treasure, the heaven to give the rain unto thy land in his season, and to bless all the work of thine hand: and thou shalt lend unto many nations, and thou shalt not borrow.”

This is the blessing that was to come upon us, “Only if thou carefully hearken unto the voice of the Lord thy God, to observe to do all these commandments”: lending to many nations and borrowing from none, reigning over many nations and none reigning over us.

Since we broke the commandments of the Most High, the other nations lend to us and we borrow from them; we go to them for loans and everything else. That is the blessing Israel forfeited by breaking the commandments.

precepts.text: Ye have the poor always with you; poverty does not cease, so the commandment is to open thine hand to thy poor brother.
precepts.point: The poor shall never cease out of the land; Christ said the same, that the poor are always going to be among us. That is why no campaign can fight poverty out of existence: Christ said it will always be among us.

note.label: Deuteronomy 15: The Year of Release and the Hebrew Servant

precepts.why:
“For the poor shall never cease out of the land”. Christ said the same: “For ye have the poor always with you; but me ye have not always.” The poor are always going to be among us; poverty does not cease. That is why no campaign can fight poverty out of existence: Christ said it will always be among us.

Because the poor never cease, the commandment stands: “Thou shalt open thine hand wide unto thy brother, to thy poor, and to thy needy, in thy land.” Give him surely, and let not thine heart be grieved when thou givest, for because of this thing the Most High shall bless thee in all thy works. Beware of the thought in a wicked heart that the seventh year, the year of release, is at hand, and thine eye be evil against thy poor brother; if he cry unto the Lord against thee, it is sin unto thee.

Notice that Esau had this Bible, these commandments and these laws, yet worked us to death for over four hundred years, and when they released us we did not go out with anything. They had these laws written before them and did not do them.

precepts.text: If thy brother that dwelleth by thee be waxen poor and be sold unto thee; the Hebrew sold himself to his brother when he fell poor.
precepts.point: The reason given is memory: remember that thou wast a bondman in the land of Egypt, and the Lord thy God redeemed thee.

note.label: Deuteronomy 15: The Year of Release and the Hebrew Servant

precepts.why:
Who is the Hebrew man or Hebrew woman sold unto thee? Leviticus 25 says: “And if thy brother that dwelleth by thee be waxen poor, and be sold unto thee; thou shalt not compel him to serve as a bondservant”. The Hebrew sold himself to his brother when he fell poor.

When people say slavery was taking place in Africa among us, it was not slavery like we suffered: it was people among us that fell poor and sold themselves to their brothers, the very case this law and Leviticus 25 govern.

He served six years, and in the seventh year he went free, and not empty: furnished liberally out of the flock, the floor, and the winepress, with some of the flock, the corn, and the wine. He cannot go out poor the way he came in; that shows you the Most High is a good God. And the reason given is memory: remember that thou wast a bondman in the land of Egypt, and the Lord thy God redeemed thee.

precepts.text: Do not harden your heart or shut your hand from your poor brother, but open your hand wide and lend him sufficient for his need.
precepts.point: When the wicked rise, men hide themselves, but when they perish the righteous increase.

note.label: Proverbs 28: The Righteous Are Bold as a Lion

precepts.why:
“He that giveth unto the poor shall not lack: but he that hideth his eyes shall have many a curse.” The law commands it: “If there be among you a poor man of one of thy brethren within any of thy gates in thy land which the Lord thy God giveth thee, thou shalt not harden thine heart, nor shut thine hand from thy poor brother: But thou shalt open thine hand wide unto him, and shalt surely lend him sufficient for his need, in that which he wanteth.”

Do not harden your heart or shut your hand from your poor brother; open your hand wide and lend him sufficient for his need. The one hiding his eyes in Proverbs is the one hardening his heart and shutting his hand here.

The law commands us to help our brothers who keep the commandments, and Sirach 12 says if you do good, know to whom you do it. If your poor brother curses you in the bitterness of his soul, his prayer is heard; open your hand and you shall not lack.

precepts.text: Thou shalt open thine hand wide unto him, and shalt surely lend him sufficient for his need.
precepts.point: Give to him that asketh thee, and from him that would borrow of thee turn not thou away. Christ is magnifying a law already written to Israel.

note.label: Matthew 5: The Sermon on the Mount and the Magnifying of the Law

precepts.why:
“Give to him that asketh thee, and from him that would borrow of thee turn not thou away.” Christ is magnifying a law already written to Israel: “But thou shalt open thine hand wide unto him, and shalt surely lend him sufficient for his need, in that which he wanteth.”

Moses warns against the thought in a wicked heart that the year of release is at hand, so that “thine eye be evil against thy poor brother, and thou givest him nought; and he cry unto the Lord against thee, and it be sin unto thee.” Instead, “Thou shalt surely give him, and thine heart shall not be grieved when thou givest unto him: because that for this thing the Lord thy God shall bless thee in all thy works”.

So Christ did not bring a new commandment about giving and lending. He magnified the law Israel already had, to open the hand wide and give without a grieved heart, and the blessing that follows it.
